Problem[edit]

Six chairs are arranged around a round table. Two students and two teachers randomly select four of the chairs to sit in. What is the probability that the two students will sit in two adjacent chairs and the two teachers will also sit in two adjacent chairs?

Solution 1 (20 seconds)[edit]

Pair two students together and put them adjacent on any two seats. There are 6 ways to do this. Considering one of these cases (they are all the same), there are 4 seats left, in which we wish to arrange the teachers together. So pair the teachers together and put them adjacent on any two seats not already occupied by two of the students. There are 3 ways to do this. For all 6 cases, there are \( 6 \times 3 = 18 \) favorable outcomes.

The number of ways to arrange the 2 students and 2 teachers is .

Our probability is \( \frac{18}{90} = \)

~Pinotation

Solution quick (15 seconds)[edit]

We can treat the \(2\) students, \(2\) teachers, and \(2\) empty chairs as \(6\) distinct objects arranged around a circular table. The total number of unique circular arrangements, accounting for rotational symmetry, is: \((6-1)!=5!\) To find the number of favorable arrangements, we group the two students into one object and the two teachers into another object. Combined with the \(2\) distinct empty chairs, we have a total of \(4\) objects to arrange around the circular table. The number of ways to arrange these \(4\) objects in a circle is: \((4-1)!=3!\) We must now account for the internal arrangements within each group. The two students can switch seats in \(2!\) ways, and the two teachers can switch seats in \(2!\) ways. The probability is therefore: \(\frac{3!\cdot 2!\cdot 2!}{5!}=\boxed{\frac{1}{5}}\) ~Aar_v

We consider how many ways there are to place the students and teachers at random at the table. This is a word arrangement in a circle, and so there are different ways of doing so, assuming that teachers, students and empty spaces are indistinguishable between themselves.

Now, we wish to find how many favorable arrangments there are, so suppose we fix two adjacent teachers. Then, there are three "spots" (blocks of two seats) two adjacent students could occupy: two on the side of either teacher, and one such that no student is sitting adjacent to a teacher.

Thus, the probability is .
